analysis.one_liner: Cuts off ICE funds for biometric surveillance systems and new hires until the agency discloses its database policies.
analysis.headline: Introduced by a single House Democrat with no cosponsors, the bill has sat in two House committees without a hearing or vote since February 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would freeze ICE's ability to spend money on biometric and other surveillance systems, including its Intelligence Records System, and on hiring new officers, until the Department of Homeland Security submits a detailed report explaining what data those systems collect, who can see it, how long it is kept, and how it protects information gathered from people exercising constitutional rights. It would also require deleting data collected by immigration officers since January 1, 2026 unless the new policy is adopted, and would bar the government from using funds to stop people from lawfully recording ICE operations. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary and Homeland Security committees and sent to a Homeland Security subcommittee, where it has remained without action.
analysis.who_benefits: Immigrants and anyone whose information ends up in ICE's surveillance databases, including people who have protested or exercised First Amendment rights; bystanders who want to record enforcement operations; and communities subject to ICE raids who would gain notice, correction, and deletion rights over information about them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Immigrants, protesters, and people in ICE databases

how_it_helps.text: The bill would block spending on ICE's biometric and other surveillance systems, including the Intelligence Records System, and on hiring additional ICE officers until DHS submits a report on how those systems are governed [S2].

The required report must include a policy barring use of information collected from a person because they exercised a constitutional right, plus rules on who can access the data, how long it is kept, and how people can review, contest, or remove their own information [S2].
It would require deletion of data collected by immigration officers between January 1, 2026 and enactment, unless the Secretary adopts the new policy within 30 days [S2].
It would prohibit using any federal funds to stop an individual from recording or documenting ICE enforcement operations, so long as the recording does not obstruct them [S2].

analysis.who_pays: DHS and its surveillance-system contractors, who would lose contract payments and new hiring authority while the funding freeze lasts; ICE, which would lose some operational data and staffing growth; and, per critics, potentially some enforcement capability.

drawbacks.text: The funding cutoff is broad: it freezes not only surveillance systems but also all hiring of additional ICE officers and agents until a multi-committee report is submitted, which critics would say handcuffs an enforcement agency mid-operation with no emergency carve-out [S2].

The mandatory deletion of all data collected since January 1, 2026 could erase records from ongoing investigations and removal proceedings unless the agency completes a rulemaking within 30 days, a deadline an honest supporter would acknowledge is very tight [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real grievance: a federal surveillance system that appears to log information about people exercising constitutional rights, with the public given no clear policy on access, retention, or deletion [S2]. The trade-off is real too: an unconditional freeze on hiring and surveillance spending, plus forced data deletion, could disrupt live enforcement, and the 30-day reporting window may be unrealistic. A narrower version keyed to the report, with exceptions for public safety, would have been easier to defend.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary and Homeland Security committees and then to a Homeland Security subcommittee, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote while Congress remains in session [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Chellie Pingree introduced the bill on February 26, 2026 [S1] [S4].

The same day, it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and additionally to the House Homeland Security Committee, which sent it to its Oversight, Investigations, and Accountability Subcommittee on February 27, 2026 [S4].
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor [S3].
No further action has been recorded since the subcommittee referral; the bill has received no hearing, markup, or vote, and Congress is still in session [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because no vote has occurred, the status quo holds: ICE keeps spending on its surveillance systems, its contractors keep their contracts, and no new data or notice rules apply. Congress's Homeland Security committees also face no obligation to act on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: ICE and its surveillance contractors, so far

for.name: Rep. Chellie Pingree
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought committee consideration

sides.party_line_note: No Republican signed on and no vote has been taken, so the partisan split is untested; the bill's fate rests with the committees where it sits, both led by the House majority, and it shows no signs of reaching the floor [S3] [S4].

industries.note: The bill freezes payments for operating biometric and other surveillance systems, including the Intelligence Records System, and bars new contracts until a policy report is delivered [S2]. These contractors profit from a database that tracks people during enforcement operations, including information gathered from constitutional activity, so their financial interest runs against the transparency and deletion rights the bill would give the public [S2].

The bill freezes ICE's hiring of additional officers and agents and requires deletion of data collected in 2026 unless the agency adopts a new governance policy, reducing both staffing growth and database contents [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no hearing, and no action for months in a committee controlled by the opposing majority, the realistic path is that this bill dies quietly at the end of the Congress, like most single-sponsor bills referred to two committees.
